headline: IBC 2026 sold agents and speed. Almost nobody talked about emotion, or about whether viewers actually watch more. That is the lane to own this quarter.
summary: "Agentic" is now table stakes: at least 13 of the companies we track pitched agents at or since IBC. It no longer sets anyone apart. What the agent understands about the video still does.

Mood metadata is getting crowded (ThinkAnalytics, ContentWise, Bitmovin, PA TV Metadata, Eon Media). "We tag mood" won't stand out. Scene-level emotion that changes across the runtime, and is tied to viewing, will.
Competitor proof points are almost all about staff time saved (70%, 75%, 16 hours to 9 minutes). Viewer outcomes such as watch time, click-to-play and churn are the open lane.
CTV ad buying has started pricing ad load, attention and "emotional intensity" (FreeWheel, 17 Sep). Nobody scores where in the story the break lands, which is exactly Vionlabs' ad-break thesis.

Backdrop to react to this week: Skydance closed its WBD deal (6 Oct) and plans to merge Paramount+ and HBO Max; Disney+/Hulu prices rise on 21 Oct; HUB finds a default service is up to 6x harder to cancel.

ideas.hook: Disney+ subscribers get a 13% bigger bill tomorrow. Most won't cancel because of the price. They'll cancel the month they can't find anything to watch.
ideas.angle: Price rises raise the bar for 'was it worth it this month?'. HUB's research says being someone's default service makes you up to 6x harder to cancel, and default is won on the home screen, not with the content budget. Surfacing more of the catalogue you already own is the cheapest retention lever there is.
ideas.proof: Mood rows and Similar Titles from Curio; the 'libraries already exist' thesis. Post on 21 Oct when the price change lands.

reactsTo.label: Disney+ and Hulu raise prices again (Hawaii News Now)

ideas.hook: HBO Max and Paramount+ are about to become one app. The hard part isn't the tech stack. It's making two libraries that were never described the same way feel like one.
ideas.angle: The biggest catalogue merger in streaming is a metadata problem before it is a UX problem. Two taxonomies, two tones of voice, one home screen. Describing every title by what it feels like, scene by scene, is a common language both libraries can share.
ideas.proof: Scene-level emotion metadata as a shared layer across catalogues; Fingerprint+ embeddings. Keep it about the problem, not a pitch to Skydance.

ideas.hook: IBC was wall-to-wall agents. I didn't hear many booths explain what their agent actually understands about the film.
ideas.angle: Agents are only as good as what they can read. Gracenote's own test showed an ungrounded LLM invented every metadata attribute for 506 of 2,600 titles. Grounding in facts fixes hallucinated cast lists, but a request like 'tense but not violent' needs to know how the scenes feel. Before an agent can act on your catalogue, something has to understand it.
ideas.proof: Vionlabs showed its own Agentic Layer at IBC, so frame this as 'we build agents too, and here's what they stand on', not anti-agent.

ideas.hook: Six minutes of ads an hour beat twelve on recall by 89%. Nobody is measuring where those six minutes land in the story.
ideas.angle: FreeWheel now scores inventory on number of breaks, ad duration, clutter and emotional intensity. That's a big step. The missing variable is narrative position: a break at a natural pause and a break mid-reveal cost the viewer very different amounts. Slide by slide: the recall data, what gets scored today, what doesn't, and how a story-aware break is found.
ideas.proof: Ad-Break Creation and Contextual Ad-Breaks; SeaOvers / i-CABLE deployment; the SDVI ad-break demo at IBC.

ideas.hook: 60% of CTV bid requests don't know what show they're running in. We're building scene-level targeting on data that isn't there.
ideas.angle: Wurl, Peer39, IRIS.TV and FreeWheel's Context Engine all move contextual signals through the pipe. Peer39's own numbers say most requests arrive with nothing usable, and labels differ from publisher to publisher. The signal has to be created where the content lives, by the content owner, from the video itself.
ideas.proof: Metadata Enrichment generated from picture and sound at the source and delivered upstream; the ad-tech partner model with SeaOvers.

ideas.hook: "Mood" is on every metadata spec sheet now. Five questions that tell you whether it's real.
ideas.angle: 1. Is it derived from text (synopses, subtitles) or from picture and sound? 2. One tag per title, or per scene? 3. How was it validated? 4. Does it change across the runtime? 5. Where is it used, and what did it move? A buyer's checklist rather than a competitor attack.
ideas.proof: Show one real emotion curve across a well-known film; link the existing post 'Your AI Can See the Scene. It Can't Feel It.' Don't name competitors.

ideas.hook: Every major streamer now has a vertical feed. Only one has shared how often a clip turns into a watch, and that was for live sports.
ideas.angle: Timeline: Tubi Scenes, Peacock, Disney+ Verts, Netflix Clips, HBO Max Shorts. The feed is standard now; the contest is what goes in it and whether it pays back. Peacock's 20% tap-through into live Olympics events is the only public number. Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 is solved; choosing which 90 seconds to crop is not.
ideas.proof: Preview Clips & Shorts picks moments by emotional arc; Arash's Streaming Media Q&A on verticalization (June) for continuity.

ideas.hook: Sports has a goal. A drama doesn't. So what's the "goal" in a 90-minute film?
ideas.angle: Sports clipping works because events are tagged: goal, penalty, red card. Drama has no scoreboard, which is why entertainment lags sports in automated clips. The equivalent of a goal is an emotional turn: the moment tension breaks, the reveal, the laugh. Show the difference between an event timeline and an emotion curve for the same film.
ideas.proof: An emotion curve for one title with the auto-picked preview moment marked on it.

ideas.hook: Saving an editor 70% of their time is a cost story. Getting a viewer to watch one more title is a revenue story. Our industry keeps pitching the first one.
ideas.angle: Read the IBC proof points: 70% less search time, 16 hours down to 9 minutes, 50% faster. All real, all about the back office. The one viewer-side number that stood out came from ThinkAnalytics: over 30% more viewing from carousels once the metadata improved. Better inputs beat a better ranking model. Why Vionlabs measured viewer outcomes from day one.
ideas.proof: Needs one public Vionlabs viewer-outcome number (engagement or click-to-play lift). Check with sales which case can be cited.

ideas.hook: Most recommendation engines are built for the viewer with 2,000 hours of history. We built Curio for the one who has watched two titles.
ideas.angle: Cold start is the problem nobody in discovery wrote about this autumn. It hits hardest at small and regional services that will never have Netflix-scale behavioural data. Signals from the content itself level that field: day one, two titles watched, and the rows already reflect a mood.
ideas.proof: Curio launch with Great American Pure Flix (public); the day-one mood-rows visual from the Curio landing page.

ideas.hook: News is the fastest-growing FAST genre, up 53% in a year. It's also the genre where one badly placed ad break ends up as a screenshot.
ideas.angle: Gracenote counts 2,172 FAST channels, with news up 52.9% and Europe (UK +21.3%, Germany +21.5%) growing faster than the US. A car ad after a crash report, a holiday ad after a disaster story: contextual breaks matter most where the content is most sensitive. Speaks straight to the news-broadcaster ICP.

gaps.title: Viewer outcomes, not editor speed
gaps.detail: Nearly every competitor proof point measures staff time or output volume. Almost none report watch time, click-to-play, completion or churn. The exceptions are ThinkAnalytics (+30% carousel viewing) and Peacock (20% tap-through from highlights, sports only). Whoever publishes viewer-side numbers first owns this.

evidence.label: Moments Lab: Studio and MXT at IBC
yallo adds AI previews with Media Distillery

gaps.title: Emotion across the runtime
gaps.detail: No competitor item from September or October uses emotion language for discovery or clipping. Mood shows up only as a title-level tag or an ad-inventory score. The emotional arc of a title, scene by scene and validated against viewing, is unclaimed.

gaps.title: Where the break lands in the story
gaps.detail: FreeWheel now scores ad load, clutter and emotional intensity, and Bitmovin places SCTE-35 markers at scene boundaries for Nine. Nobody scores the narrative position of a break or what it costs the viewer. That's the ad-break detection thesis, almost word for word.

gaps.title: The signal at the source
gaps.detail: Contextual CTV players are pipes: Wurl, IRIS.TV and Peer39 move signals, and Peer39 says about 60% of requests carry no program signal. AI buying agents (Magnite, LG, NBCU) will need structured scene and emotion data to read. Vionlabs can position as where that signal is created.

gaps.title: Choosing the moment, not cropping it
gaps.detail: Vertical tools sell auto-crop, speed and one-click publishing (Comcast, Qvest + Nvidia, Moments Lab, OpusClip). HBO Max still has humans review the clips its AI picks. Nobody claims a better way to choose which moment, or proves the clip led to a full watch.

gaps.title: Back-catalogue value for your own subscribers
gaps.detail: "Archive monetisation" now means licensing footage out (Veritone with ATP, data marketplaces) or cutting social clips. Nobody argues for bringing back-catalogue titles back in front of existing subscribers, which is the 'libraries already exist' thesis.

evidence.label: Moments Lab: A+E from archive to feed

gaps.title: Cold start and smaller streamers
gaps.detail: No 2026 discovery-vendor content addresses new or long-tail titles without viewing history, or services without behavioural scale. XroadMedia owns 'sovereign' discovery but frames it as regulation and culture, not data scarcity. Curio is built for exactly this.

evidence.label: XroadMedia IBC panel on rules and regulation
